chunks: When external termination is needed. The question: When would you need external termination components?
External termination is a resistor you add to stop signals from bouncing back and forth on a trace.
You need it only when the trace is long compared with the edge speed, the driver and receiver are not matched to the line, and the bouncing would break the receiver's limits.
Short, slow traces and chips with built-in termination do not need it.
Think of shouting down a corridor with a wall at the end. In a very short corridor the echo returns while you are still shouting, so it blends in.
In a long corridor you hear a separate echo. A pillow on the far wall (termination) kills it. You only need the pillow in a long corridor.
Start with electrical length, then check whether the mismatch actually produces a problem. Terminate only if the answer to the last question is no.
The shortcut at the top removes most nets on a board.
Electrical length: the trace delay compared with the rise time. It is "long" when the delay is more than t r over 6 ("When transmission line analysis applies").
Reflection coefficient ( ): the fraction of a wave that bounces back where the impedance changes. +1 means all of it.
Overshoot and ringing: voltage above the final level, and the oscillation from repeated reflections ("Ringing"). On-die termination (ODT): termination built into the chip.
A 1 nanoseconds edge needs termination only if the trace delay is above t r over 6 about 167 picoseconds. At about 5. 9 picoseconds per millimeter, that is about 28 mm.

"I terminate when the trace is electrically long, meaning one-way delay above about a sixth of the rise time, and the driver and receiver aren't matched, so reflections would cause overshoot or ringing beyond the receiver's limits and noise margin.
That's typical for fast clocks, multi-drop buses, differential and high-speed links, and anything with an EMI problem.
I skip it for short, slow nets and for receivers with on-die termination, and I choose series termination when power matters and parallel when I need a clean wave along the line."
